review.reason: Read collection, standardization, dating assumptions, results, and alternative explanations. Teaches how archaeological proxies reveal—and obscure—trade.

item.title: Unpacking Roman trade: a quantitative study of amphora circulation in the Western provinces
item.headline: Roman shipping jars trace changing food trade
item.authors: Cèsar Carreras, Tom Brughmans, Pau de Soto Cañamares, and Daniel Blumenkranz
item.summary: Shipping jars from 216 western Roman sites reveal changing trade in wine, oil, and fish sauce. Fewer surviving jars need not mean less commerce.

evidence.question: How did Roman food distribution change?
evidence.method: Compared 20 amphora types across 254 excavations, standardizing by excavated area and distributing uncertain dates across their possible years.
evidence.limitations: Uneven site coverage, selected vessel types, and uniform dating assumptions shape the patterns.

explainer.finding: The sampled jars show an early imperial peak and later regional differences in imports.
explainer.method: Researchers compared vessel densities, site counts, and type diversity over time.
explainer.meaning: An olive-oil jar made in southern Spain and found in Britain helps reconstruct a long-distance supply connection.
explainer.limits: Barrels and skins leave different traces. Packaging changes or local production could partly explain declining amphora imports; jars do not measure the whole economy.
